We thank the reviewer for this critical comment. We agree that the Proterozoic would
be greatly different from the present in many aspects, and have tried our best to account
for these differences better in this revision. In the original manuscript, the initial nutrient
levels were set to the present-day levels. We now confirm that some of the nutrients
reach new state in equilibrium with the boundary conditions for the Proterozoic during
the model integration (Table S1). For example, the equilibrium nitrate level is over
three orders of magnitude lower than the present-day level due to enhanced
denitrification in the anoxic Proterozoic ocean (Fig. R2-2 above), making a N-limited
ocean to suppresses NPP (Fig. 3E-F).
The near-surface Fe reservoir also equilibrates with the input flux quickly (~100 years).
The marine Fe input was set to a higher value than the present day in the original
manuscript because of the abundant dust deposition (Table S1; Liu et al., 2020). To test
the influence of different Fe input fluxes, we performed five additional simulations (see
Methods for Sensitivity Simulation Group 6) with P fixed to 1 POL. In the first
experiment, only the Fe input from the ocean bottom (with its value the same as today)
is considered, with the atmospheric and riverine Fe inputs in the original experiments
removed (Fig. R2-5B). In this case, the Fe input flux was reduced to ~1% of our original
warm Proterozoic simulation but was still ~50% of the present-day total Fe flux. In the
other four experiments, this flux (referred to as SedFe) is further reduced to 50%,
25%, 10%, and 0% of its default value (Fig. R2-5C-F). Model results show that the ocean is
much greener than the present even if the Fe flux is only 10% SedFe (Fig. R2-5E),
indicating that Fe is not a limiting factor for the flourishing of phytoplankton when
zooplankton is absent.
The results above show that under extremely low nutrient levels (e.g., P reduced to ≤10%
POL), the biosphere could diminish so that talking about the self-shielding effect
becomes meaningless. However, as long as the nutrient level was not drastically
deficient compared to the present, as we reasoned in the original manuscript, the
Proterozoic ocean would be greener with strong self-shielding effect and less
productive than the present-day ocean.
With these new results, we agree with Reviewer #2 that our original statements
regarding the productivity understated the importance of nutrient availability. The
Proterozoic ocean could be more productive if there were a lot more P than in the
present-day ocean, in which case, the ocean would be even greener than shown in the
original manuscript (Fig. R2-4 A/G and Table S3). Understandably, the Proterozoic
ocean could be less green than the present-day ocean if the P was extremely low.
However, we think a greener but less productive ocean is still the most likely situation
for the Proterozoic. We have revised our manuscript accordingly, highlighting the
importance of nutrients in our conclusions and the effect of the greener ocean on the
subsurface productivity. Please see the texts below for the detailed responses and the
relevant revisions in the manuscript.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Review of Liu et al., NatComm
In their contribution Liu et al., explore two interesting mechanisms to throttle global
primary productivity in the Proterozoic ocean. The first is to examine the effect of
removing all predation from the Proterozoic environment, which the authors simulate
to increase production in surface waters. A consequence of this increased production is
the blocking of sunlight to deeper depths which the authors simulations suggest an
overall decrease in NPP.
Overall I found the ideas in the manuscript to be very interesting at a conceptual level,
but to lack strong grounding to be considered meaningful in forwarding our
understanding of the Proterozoic environment.
We appreciate the recognition of our idea from Reviewer #3 and are happy to make the
requested revisions, especially adding more related modern observations and additional
sensitivity simulations.
Does removing zooplankton increase surface production and thus particle density in
surface waters? The authors reference observations from the Gulf of Mexico, but is this
a general truth? For this argument to be convincing I would expect a broader
global assessment of how the ratio of zooplankton to phytoplankton impacts NPP across
many areas in the modern environment. My hunch is that there is much more complexity in
such interactions than is presented in the current manuscript.
We thank Reviewer #3 for this constructive suggestion. And yes, removing
zooplankton could increase surface production and chlorophyll substantially as
demonstrated in the new sensitivity simulation where we added zooplankton back to
the Proterozoic ocean (Fig. R3-1A-D; see Methods for Sensitivity Simulation Group 1).
However, the total NPP would decrease in the zooplankton-involved simulation
because zooplankton would consume a large amount of nutrients, leading to a nutrient-
limited (in particular, nitrate) ocean and suppressing NPP (Fig. R3-1E-F).
We have also added more modern observations about this phenomenon in different
regions through a broader literature review. In the Aleutian archipelago and Alaska of
the North Pacific, the collapse of herbivores (including zooplankton) due to the
presence of sea otters would enhance kelp abundance and production of autotrophs
(Estes and Duggins, 1995; Estes et al., 2011). A greener region of Long Lake in
Michigan with abundant phytoplankton was observed when experimentally removing
the largemouth bass. Because this bass preys on smaller zooplanktivorous fishes,
removing the bass will decrease zooplankton and thus increase phytoplankton
(Carpenter et al., 2001; Estes et al., 2011; Fig. R3-2). The predatory spotted bass, eating
herbivorous minnows, could promote the growth of algae as observed in Oklahoma
streams (Power et al., 1985). In the open ocean of the North Pacific, the abundance of
fish (e.g., salmon and saury) would cause the decline of zooplankton and thus enhance
the growth of phytoplankton (Odate, 1994; Shiomoto et al., 1997). The above examples
are mostly triggered by the apex (large) consumers and could cause the following chain
effects through feed webs, noted as “trophic cascades” (Estes et al., 2011).
Unfortunately, no information on the quantitative change of NPP could be found for
these events.
The reviewer is correct that the interactions listed above are more complex in modern
Earth with more than two species involved and may include tipping points, around
which abrupt changes in ecosystem structure and function may occur (Scheffer et al.,
2001). The response of the Proterozoic ocean ecosystem to zooplankton removal is also
more complex than thought in the original manuscript. The presence of zooplankton
decreases the total NPP with the major reason being that nitrate (N) nutrient is also
consumed by this species; the ecosystem became N limited under the Proterozoic low-
N background (Fig. R3-1E), which itself was due to the low pO and thus enhanced
2
denitrification in the ocean.
We now summarize the reasons for the generally lower global NPP in the Proterozoic
ocean as: 1) the absence of diatom reduces the global NPP by ~20% according to the
present-day budget. 2) the much lower N nutrient level due to the low O level
2
would drive a low total NPP even if the biospheric composition was similar to today.
3) without zooplankton consuming N, the productivity would not be limited by N but
the self-shielding effect would then prevent the NPP from increasing significantly.
We have added the above discussion in the revised manuscript and pasted below.

We have also added more observations related to the shielding phenomenon in modern

decrease when the biomass of overshielding plankton increases, even though
microphytobenthos can persist at low light levels. For example, the enhanced shielding

Bucht are about 2 and 10 times lower than those of Rossower Strom due to the light
limitation as indicated by in situ and laboratory data (Meyercordt and Meyer-Reil,

With the above comments in mind, I also think it is worth noting on whether such results
are truly relevant to the Proterozoic, a 2 billion year interval of Earth’s past. The authors
use a single continental configuration, however, this would have varied considerably
across this eon. Moreover, the authors appear to have ignored virtually all geochemical
data across this interval in their analysis and instead have opted to take modern values
and explore how they might change with a different continental configuration and the
imposed effects of no zooplankton. For example, if productivity was lower globally due
to P limitation or metal limitation which may have decreased the rate of nitrogenase
synthesis, would the self shielding effect still matter?
We appreciate Reviewer #3 for these constructive suggestions. Although only the
continental reconstruction for 720 Ma is used in this study, the characteristics of the
ecosystem for the whole Proterozoic may be considered fundamentally similar given
that the continents were located relatively in the low latitudes for the whole Eon (Cao
et al., 2024; Li et al., 2008). Moreover, we have conducted 17 additional sensitivity
simulations in this revision, which should be sufficient to cover the uncertainties due to
continental configurations. For example, the influence of different oceanic dust
deposition under different continental configurations should not be greater than that in
the sensitivity experiment where all dust deposition was removed (see Methods for
Sensitivity Simulation Group 6). Similarly, the influence of continental silicate
weathering and the associated riverine nutrient input may be covered by the sensitivity
tests in which the phosphorus (P) concentration in the ocean was changed (see Methods
for Sensitivity Simulation Group 5). The P concentration has been changed from 2.5%
present oceanic level (POL) to 500% POL according to geological evidence (Guilbaud
et al., 2020; Planavsky et al., 2010). The results of these simulations show that the most
critical driving mechanism for the simulated greener Proterozoic ocean is the absence
of zooplankton (Fig. R3-1A) rather than other factors, including the continental
configuration.
The reviewer is correct that the self-shielding effect would not matter anymore if the
nutrient level is very low. For example, if P concentration in the Proterozoic was 10%
POL or lower, the surface productivity would be too low to trigger the self-shielding
effect (Fig. R3-3E-F and K-L) and the sunlight was no longer be the key limiting factor
for phytoplankton (Fig. R3-4). However, such low P (i.e. 2.5% PAL) concentration is
a lower bound of the available reconstructions (Guilbaud et al., 2020). We may consider
that the Proterozoic ocean was most likely greener and the self-shielding effect was
strong. We have added the above discussion in the revised manuscript and pasted below.

surface remains slightly greener than the PI ocean surface (Fig. S15D and Table S3).

than twice or less than one fourth of the PI level (i.e., 1 POL).

indicate that the Proterozoic ocean would be greener but less productive for the most
likely ranges (25% POL < P < 200% POL, and loose ranges for N and Fe) of nutrients
levels.

We sincerely thank Reviewer #3 for the highly constructive comments, which help us
improve the quality of the manuscript. We have added broader observations about the
effects of the absence of zooplankton on the phytoplankton and production to support
our findings. Moreover, we have also carried out additional sensitivity tests to clarify
the driving factors of the greener ocean and the potential effects of different nutrient
scenarios in the Proterozoic. We hope our efforts and modifications are appropriate to
address the concerns of Reviewer #3 and may provide new knowledge to the field
through numerical simulations.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Review of “A Greener but Less Productive Proterozoic Ocean” by Liu et al. for Nature
Communications.
After reviewing the revised manuscript and the authors’ responses to the reviewers’
comments, I am encouraged to see that the main scientific concerns raised in the initial
review have been addressed. The revisions have improved the manuscript, and the
results are interesting and valuable to the community.
That said, I believe the manuscript would benefit from another careful pass focused
specifically on language and framing. In its current form, the text is often difficult to
follow, and some statements read as more definitive than is warranted given the
uncertainties associated with the Proterozoic. Improving clarity and tone is important
here because the conclusions rely on subtle modeling arguments, which risk being
obscured or misinterpreted when the language is imprecise or overly strong.
I therefore recommend publication contingent on further language revisions aimed at
improving coherence, precision, and appropriate qualification of uncertainty. Below I
list several specific examples to guide the authors. This list is not exhaustive, but it
illustrates the types of changes that are still needed throughout the manuscript.
We appreciate Reviewer #2 for the supportive comments and kind recognition of our
efforts in the last revision. We agree with the reviewer that careful and rational
interpretation of results is critical, and have thus modified the manuscript throughout,
focusing on the precision and objectivity during the presentation of our results. Please
see the following responses to the specific suggestions raised by the reviewer and the
other related modifications made to the manuscript regarding the diction.
1. Line 25: The phrase “under the most probable nutrient levels” is too casual for a
scientific article. Please consider rephrasing to something more explicit, for example:

nutrient regimes” in line 92.

added “reaching” in line 165.

derived origin of results throughout the manuscript to improve the overall clarity and
objectivity of our presentation (e.g., line 97, 181, etc.).
4. Line 38: “considerable” is vague and not very informative. A more precise term such
as “substantial” would be preferable. It would also help to explicitly state the ranges
discussed in previous studies, for example: “… might have been substantial (between
A and B in the Proterozoic, compared to C today)”.

from poor presentation and presenting certain simulations as their preferred scenario to
attempt to constrain features of the Proterozoic environment such as primary
productivity and depths of the chlorophyll max, which does not reflect the full degree
of the uncertainty that is explored in their simulations. Again, I believe the ideas are
interesting in this manuscript, however in it's current form it does not seem to add new
constraints, but rather possible consequences of posited nutrient levels across the
Proterozoic. Therefore I am not supportive of the publication of this work in its current
form.
We appreciate Reviewer #3 for the re-evaluation of the manuscript and kind recognition
of our efforts in the last revision. We apologize for certain imprecise interpretations of
our findings, which have also been pointed out by other reviewers. To address the
comments of Reviewer #3, the following revisions and clarifications have been
implemented in the revised manuscript.
(1) We have widely used the past conditional tense to reflect uncertainty and improve
objectivity, especially in the result presentations. For example, we have changed “could
be” to “could have been” in line 47; used “may have affected” instead of “might affect”
in line 48. Please see the revised manuscript for other modifications related to this type
of issue (e.g., line 62, 106, etc.).
(2) We have clarified the model-derived origin in the result presentation to avoid
misinterpretation of our findings. For example, we have added “Simulation results
show that” before the original “without grazing by zooplankton…” in line 100. Please
see the revised manuscript for the complete modifications following this logic (e.g.,
line 111,119, etc.).
(3) More importantly, we wish to clarify that the ranges of nutrients selected in our
simulations (Table S1 and S2) were bounded by geological observations and model
constraints. Specifically, the marine phosphorus level might be between 2.5% to 500%
of the present oceanic level (POL) based on geochemical records (Guilbaud et al., 2020;
Planavsky et al., 2010); the marine nitrogen level might have been determined by the
marine (de)nitrification, which would have been largely affected by atmospheric
oxygen level (pO ). Thus, we have tested the range of pO from 0.1% to 10% of the
2 2
present level based on geological records and model studies (Lyons et al., 2014). Our
model would dynamically iterate the nitrogen level to the equilibrium state accordingly,
which is also consistent with the Proterozoic situation as demonstrated by previous
works (Kang et al., 2023; Motomura et al., 2023); the iron inputs have also been set
based on geological records and model simulations (Liu et al., 2020; Watanabe et al.,
2023). Thus, the selected nutrient levels and characteristics of the ecosystem simulated
by the state-of-the-art GCM model might be plausible for the Proterozoic.
(4) After conducting the sensitivity tests, the uncertainty in nitrogen and iron within the
expected ranges has almost no influence on the simulated greener and less productive
Proterozoic ocean (Fig. S13 and S16). However, model results would show a more
productive (still greener) Proterozoic ocean under high (>200% POL) phosphorus
levels, and a less green (still less productive) Proterozoic ocean under extremely low
(<25% POL) phosphorus levels (Fig. S15). Those simulation results have all been
discussed in the section “Uncertainties in the simulated surface greening and NPP”.
Moreover, to highlight and reflect the full degree of the simulation results, we have
added the following contexts in the summary section of the revised manuscript.
Line 312-314: It is noted that a less green or more productive Proterozoic ocean might
be plausible when the phosphorus level was less than one fourth or more than twice of
the PI level, respectively.
At last, we sincerely thank Reviewer #3 again for the constructive comments, and hope
our modifications are appropriate to address the reviewer’s concerns.
